steps.text: Beat egg whites in a clean glass or metal bowl with an electric mixer on high speed until stiff peaks form. Set aside.
Beat egg yolks, buttermilk, flour, melted butter, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and salt together in a large bowl until well combined. Gently fold in egg whites.
Heat an aebleskiver pan over medium heat. Add about 1 tablespoon vegetable oil to the bottom of each cup.

Pour about 2 tablespoons batter into each prepared cup. When bubbles appear around edges, quickly flip (Danish cooks use a long knitting needle, but a fork will work). Continue turning the ball to keep it from burning until cooked through.

raw_recipe.headline: Aebleskiver
raw_recipe.description: Aebleskiver are light Danish pancake balls cooked in a cast-iron pan on the stovetop at Advent. They're served warm with syrup, jam, or powdered sugar

review.reviewBody:
Never use oil, only butter in the pan. The name in danish is Æbleskiver which means Appleslices (I know they're not slices, but that's the name). So if you want to make them like we do in Denmark, and always have done, you need to put a piece of apple in every one of them. 
When they're done cooking on one side put a small piece of skinless apple in to the middle, turn them around with a knitting needle to finish cooking them on the other side. You can also use applesauce instead.
Time to eat them, dip them in your favorite jam (we use jam from nordic berries like strawberry, my favorite), then dip them in icing sugar, eat and enjoy.
We're not only eating them at Christmas but at any occasion. More traditional Christmas cookies are ``Klejner (don't know what to call them in english)´´ and ``Pebernødder (peppernuts)´´.
I'll post recipes later.

Though I was raised in the US, I'm half-Danish and have lived in Denmark so I know æbleskiver! This is a good recipe, though I have two small recommendations: 1) Add a little cardamom to make it more traditional. 2) An extra egg white won't hurt if you want them to be a little fluffier. 

One more thing - use butter for the pan! It's part of what makes æbleskiver taste so delicious. Make sure the butter is clarified or it will burn. To clarify butter, slowly heat it until it bubbles and all the white solids rise to the top, then gently skim them off (cheesecloth is the preferred method if you want to do a really good job). I also recommend that you use unsalted butter because it is typically fresher than salted butter.

We made these this morning, with no changes to the main recipe, and they were delicious!
A couple notes though - 
I tried butter, oil and then pam spray in the pan, and the spray worked out the best. With the melted butter in the batter, a touch of spray in the pan worked great.
We have two boys, so I thought it would be a safe bet to increase the recipe by 50% so we would have enough. That wasn’t necessary at all, the original recipe makes plenty. We had to toss a bunch of batter.
I used a heaping teaspoon of batter, then dropped some Nutella into the center, then covered it up with about a half teaspoon or so. I sprayed a touch of pam spray on top so they would be lubed up before flipping, and sprinkled some powdered sugar on them while they were cooling. 
I’ll post pictures in a moment, but they were just delicious.

My husband said that we don't need to wait until Christmas to have these again! :) I added a teaspoon of cardamom for a Scandinavian flavor. Delicious! I served these with the choice of blueberry sauce, powdered sugar and/or cream cheese frosting. (I warmed the frosting so it was more like a glaze. I bought the Lodge cast iron pan from Amazon. I did not put an entire T of butter in each well, probably a teaspoon or less each time and they turned out very well. I turned them with a chopstick. I think I'll go have another! So yummy. If you don't have an Aebleskiver pan, the batter would be great as a waffle!

I have made this recipe dozens (if not hundreds) of times. They are a favorite of my family. I like to use a mini Aebleskiver plan and put a chocolate chip in each one for the kids. Also they are best if you dust them with powdered sugar on top just before serving. If I do not have any buttermilk handy I have substituted with 1.5 C milk, 1T apple cider vinegar, and .5 C yogurt and they turn out great.

DO NOT SUB ANYTHING FOR THE BUTTERMILK! Milk with lemon juice makes sour milk, not buttermilk. I feel like I can give a pretty good review after using this recipe three times. The first time I made these I didn't have quite enough buttermilk so I used 1/2 cup of milk with 1 1/2 cups of buttermilk. Although tasty, in the end, they were not pretty and I made a huge mess because the batter was a bit runny. The second and third times I made these I noticed a big difference in the thickness of the batter using all buttermilk. It was more like muffin batter except fluffier. I used a cookie dough scooper to transfer the batter from the bowl to the pan. The only change to the recipe each time is that I did not use one tablespoon of oil in each well. If I had, there would not have been any room for batter. I used about 1/4 teaspoon of clarified butter in each well and then used a silicone pastry brush to make sure that not only the wells were covered but also the entire top of the pan because the batter does puff up and sometimes overrun the wells. About the fillings: we found that we like them plain with a sprinkle of powdered sugar and a choice of toppings. Some like thinned jam and others like maple or pancake syrup. Thank you Lisa G.!

Highly recommend using melted butter (clarified not necessary) rather than vegetable oil, and to limit the amount to about 2 teaspoons butter to 1 tablespoon of batter in the aebleskiver pan. A bit more sugar in the batter is also quite pleasant. Pre-cooked apple piece in the center is brilliant and traditional, and all soft or pre-cooked fruits, Nutella, and similar make for lovely fillings as the mood moves you. Give them a bit more time than you first think in cooking.

Since I cannot stand for very long, I have used Krusteaz pancake mix, adding two eggs, some cinnamon and nutmeg, Turning them a quarter turn first time, then adding a teaspoonful of home style applesauce, then turning it again. Following one last half turn I remove them from the pan and while hot drop them into a bag with cinnamon sugar, shake well, then serve. Sometimes will not use the cinnamon sugar but will serve them up then drizzle a little clover honey over them. Have filled them home made elderberry, blackberry, boysenberry or apple jelly, these I might sprinkle with just a very light coating of powdered sugar or just drizzle some warmed jelly over them. Have them whenever I have the hunger for them. Developed a taste for them at the Junction City Scandinavian Festival, where I got my first pan. Had to give them up for almost 30 years while I traveled the world for Uncle Sam, kind of hard to carry cooking supplies in a seabag. I am of Danish and Swedish Viking, and Prussian ancestry. So I love the foods and drinks from those areas.

These were outstanding! I’ve made Æbleskiver before, but the recipe I have previously used had a very pancakey taste. Not this recipe. This recipe produces light, moist, tender pillows of goodness. My 2 year old insisted they were “doughnuts”.

 I followed the recipe with precision. But I also added 2-3 blueberries inside each before turning, and after removing them from the pan, I brushed them with melted butter and rolled them in cinnamon sugar (I think that might be the “doughnut” connection).

The hardest part of this recipe was getting used to the aebleskiver pan. I found that a 1/8 cup measuring cup was just about perfect scoop for the batter. I looked at other recipes and one had some cardamom in the recipe and added it to mine. While these were still warm, I drizzled honey over these pancakey, donuty little gems. I will be making these again!

Great fun to make and delicious! I followed the recipe exactly and added 1 tsp of vanilla. I am Scandinavian (Swedish and Norwegian) and was given my Aebleskiver pan for Christmas. I couldn't wait to give it a try! They are a cross between donut holes and pancakes. The recipe states to turn them quickly (which I did the first two times I made them), but after doing some research I have learned that if you turn the pancake onto its side for about 30 seconds before completely turning over to the otherside, it will produce a more round shape. It does make a difference. I used the point of two steak knifes to turn them (I couldn't find my knitting needles!), and then a spoon to remove them when done. I can't wait to make them for my grandchildren!

The best recipe, I make them every Christmas morning. My parents started the tradition and now my grown kids do it. It’s so good when my ex-wife left so took my best pan to continue my tradition for herself and hers.

I grew up eating aebleskiver as my parents were Danish immigrants. This recipe is pretty authentic. We ate them with our favorite flavor of jam. Sometimes my mom would put a dab of jam in the middle before the first flip, thus encapsulating the jam inside. We also dusted them with powdered sugar. Such a treat!

This recipe is perfect!! I’ve used it about 50 times probably! Going to finally print it off and put it in our family cookbook. Thank you so much for sharing. I wouldn’t change a thing about it. When I cook The ableskivers I use a non-stick pan, only put 1tsp oil per each cup in the pan and use 1/4 cup measuring cup for the batter. They come out great every time!
I had never heard of this before but I love it!! It was fun to make and tasted great, I will make this again! They puffed up a little bit and also had good texture.
Family tradition ❤️ but with sliced apples.

These were like little pillows, so soft and light. I tried to put some filling in a few of them like some suggested but it reduced the pilloweynesss. So I just did them plain and put something on them after, but they didn’t need it. I did do butter over oil, which added to the richness. This will be my new go to recipe. Now off to clean the kitchen. Ugh.
Just like my great-grandma use to make!
My great-grandfather was from Denmark. We always ate these with applesauce. Using real butter and beating the egg whites separately is the key.

First time making aebleskiver, and I'm a bona fide convert. These little handheld pancakes are awesome! I served them with some apple preserves, a drizzle of syrup, and some powdered sugar. Next time, I'll be brave and try stuffing the center with the preserves for easier eating! It does take a second to get the hang of it—look for edges that have pulled away from the sides before flipping. Didn't love using a fork, so swapped in chopsticks... until I remembered my stash of knitting needles!
